text: Nostalgia is the warm, slightly sad feeling of missing a time you loved and cannot get back. It is not about a place you could go to, but about the way things used to be. The article says nostalgia is part of why some musicians ban phones: Sir Paul McCartney liked that a phone-free show felt like concerts did before every crowd held up a screen.

Something ephemeral lasts only a short while and then is gone for good, like the first snow of the year or a sandcastle before the tide. The word does not say whether the thing is good or bad, only that it will not stay. The article argues that a concert nobody films is ephemeral in exactly that way: it happens once, and afterwards it exists only in the memories of the people who were there.

To heighten something is to make it stronger or more intense, and you can hear the word height sitting inside it. You heighten a feeling or a risk, not usually an object. The article points out a strange side effect of phone-free shows: if the only way to see one is to stand in the room, that may heighten the fear of missing out in everyone who is not there.

Watch this word carefully, because the article uses it in two different ways. A growing band of musicians means a group of people who are doing the same thing, which has nothing to do with music. The other use, the distance between the crowd and the band, is the musical one you already know.

To croon is to sing in a soft, low, gentle voice, the kind you lean in to hear rather than one that fills a stadium. Saying that Phoebe Bridgers croons a line tells you how it sounds, not just that she sang it. Writers use it a lot for quiet, emotional singing.

A metaphor is when you call one thing by the name of another thing to show what the two have in common. You do not say a goalkeeper is like a wall, you just say he is a wall, and everyone understands that nothing gets past him. The article wonders whether the machine in the song is a real smartphone or a metaphor for governments and big companies.

The establishment means the people and organisations already in charge: governments, big companies, the powerful groups that set the rules. It is usually said by someone who is complaining about them. The band Rage Against the Machine used the machine to mean exactly that.

Stunted means stopped from growing to full size. A plant kept in a tiny pot is stunted. Here it describes growing up: stunted maturity means someone who has not grown up as much as their age would suggest.

A gadget is a small clever device that does a particular job, like a phone, a smartwatch or a games console. The word carries a hint that the thing is fiddly or fashionable. In the article the gadgets are simply the smartphones everyone brings to concerts.

A gig is a live music performance, especially by a band or singer playing one night in one venue. Musicians use the word constantly, so journalists writing about music do too. It can also mean any short piece of paid work, which is where the phrase gig economy comes from.

A pouch is a small soft bag, usually with a flap or a drawstring that closes it. A kangaroo has one, and so does the case fans drop their phones into at these concerts. The pouch in the article locks shut with a magnet and the fan carries it around all evening.

The duration of something is how long it lasts from start to finish. For the duration of the gig means the whole time the concert is on, not a second less. You will meet this word constantly in science, sport and school timetables.

To enforce a rule is to actually make people follow it, rather than just announcing it and hoping. A referee enforces the rules of a game; a school enforces its phone policy by collecting phones. The article says Phoebe Bridgers is not alone in enforcing such rules, meaning other musicians really do lock the phones away.

Here barred has nothing to do with a chocolate bar or a metal bar. To bar something is to forbid it or block it from coming in, the way a heavy bar across a door keeps people out. Sir Paul McCartney barred phones at two concerts, meaning he did not allow them.

A yearning is a deep, aching wish for something you do not have, stronger than simply wanting it. People yearn for home, for a person, or for a time that has passed. The article says phone-free concerts are not just a yearning for simpler times, meaning there is a practical reason too, not only longing.

To aver something is to state it firmly, as a thing you are sure is true. It is a formal word that shows up in news writing and in courtrooms, where it is close to swearing something is so. Artists aver that concerts should be enjoyed in the moment means they say it firmly and mean it.

An enthusiast is someone who is really into a particular thing and knows a lot about it: a train enthusiast, a chess enthusiast. It is a friendly word, not a mocking one. At a concert, fellow enthusiasts means the other people in the room who love the same music you do.

Something disposable is made to be used and then thrown away, like paper plates or a plastic fork. A disposable camera holds one roll of film, takes about 27 photos, and is handed in to be developed. Harry Styles gave them out so fans could still take pictures without a screen in the way.

Scarcity means there is not much of something to go around. Economists use the word constantly, because scarcity is what makes things valuable: rare trading cards cost more than common ones. The article says a concert you cannot film creates scarcity, because the only copy of the experience is the one in your head.

Exclusivity is the quality of being open to only a few people and shut to everyone else. A club with a waiting list has it; a public park does not. Musicians argue that the exclusivity of a phone-free show, where you had to be there to see it, is part of what makes it feel special.

To say something bluntly is to say it plainly and directly, without softening it to be polite. A blunt knife is dull rather than sharp, and blunt speech works the same way: no careful edges. The DJ Kaytranada put it bluntly when he said a crowd of phones looks awkward from the stage.

This is not iron or steel. Metal here is a style of rock music, short for heavy metal, known for loud distorted guitars, fast drums and a dramatic stage show. Ghost, the group in the article, is a Swedish metal band.

The front man of a band is the member who stands at the front, usually the lead singer, and does the talking between songs. They are the face of the group, so reporters quote them. Ghost's front man is the one who complained about the distance he felt between the crowd and the band.

In mad awkward, mad does not mean angry or crazy. It is slang for very, used the way you might say seriously awkward or super awkward. Kaytranada is a young Canadian DJ, so he writes the way people talk.

To kick off is to begin, borrowed from the kick that starts a football match. A tour that kicks off on September 14th starts on that date. You will hear it about seasons, meetings and celebrations, not just sport.

If something plays a part in a decision, it is one of the reasons behind it but not the only one. The phrase is a careful way of saying this mattered without claiming it mattered most. Nostalgia plays a part means it is one reason musicians ban phones, and the article then gives others.

The fear of missing out is the uneasy feeling that something great is happening somewhere without you, often shortened to FOMO. It is the reason people check a group chat they do not really want to read. The article notes that a concert nobody can film may make this feeling stronger, not weaker.

A sea of something means a huge spread of it stretching as far as you can look, like water. A sea of iPhones is what a performer sees from the stage: hundreds of little bright screens instead of faces. It is a standard English phrase you will meet often, as in a sea of red jerseys.

To be in the moment is to pay full attention to what is happening right now instead of recording it, planning, or worrying. It is the opposite of watching a concert through your own phone screen. Artists in the article argue that music is meant to be appreciated in the moment.

Phoebe Bridgers is an American singer-songwriter known for quiet, sad, sharply written songs. The article opens with a line from her new song Lost Boys. Her world tour, starting on September 14th, is phone-free.

Lost Boys is the new Phoebe Bridgers song the article quotes, the one with the line about a machine. The name is an old one in stories, borrowed from the children who never grow up in Peter Pan. That fits a song the article says is about not growing up.

Rage Against the Machine is an American rock band from the 1990s, famous for angry political songs. The machine in their name means governments and big companies, not an actual device. The article mentions them to ask whether Bridgers means her name the same way.
Alicia Keys is an American singer and pianist who has been making hit records since the early 2000s. She is one of the musicians who have banned smartphones at their shows.

Childish Gambino is the stage name of Donald Glover, an American rapper, singer and actor. Musicians often perform under a made-up name like this. He is another artist who has banned phones at his concerts.
Jack White is an American rock musician, best known for the band The White Stripes. He is one of the artists listed in the article as banning smartphones at gigs.

Paul McCartney was one of the Beatles, the most famous band of the 1960s, and he is still touring today. Sir is a British honour given by the king or queen for great achievement, which is why the article calls him Sir Paul. He said his phone-free Los Angeles shows felt like an old gig.

Bob Dylan is an American singer-songwriter, famous since the 1960s and one of very few musicians to win the Nobel prize in literature. His coming tour will be phone-free. He says being device-free will make each night more unique.

Harry Styles is a British pop singer who started in the group One Direction and is now hugely successful on his own. At a recent show in Manchester he made guests put their phones away and handed out disposable cameras instead.

Ghost is a Swedish metal band known for performing in costumes and face paint. They banned phones on their 2025 tour. Their front man said he could feel a growing distance between the crowd and the band.
Kaytranada is a Canadian DJ and music producer, meaning he builds tracks and plays them live for a dancing crowd. The article ends on his blunt description of playing to a room full of raised phones.

Samsung is a huge South Korean electronics company and one of the biggest makers of smartphones in the world. The article uses its figures: the average concert-goer in Britain films about 12 and a half minutes of every show.
